meta.summary:
Where it was decided: the game turned at move 15 and was lost again at move 27. At move 15 you had a good position, then Na5 let White open lines against your king. At move 27 White blundered with Kc1, which allowed Qxc3 mate.

Opening and middlegame: White's early queen sortie (Qh5, Qf3, Qd1) cost them time. You answered calmly with Nc6, g6 and Nf6, and you got a comfortable position. Trading the bishop on f3 and castling queenside was fine. The problem was that your king sat on the side where White was pushing pawns. After 14. b4 and 15. b5, you had to ask what the pawn was threatening. White wanted bxa6 to rip open the files in front of your king. Na5 looked active, but it ignored that plan. The engine preferred Na7, which keeps the b-file closed and defends. After bxa6, your king was exposed and White had real threats.

You then defended stubbornly, and White's play got hasty. At move 27, White needed to capture on d8 with cxd8=B. Instead Kc1 walked into a mate in one. White probably didn't check your checks and captures before moving.

Three lessons:

1. When the enemy pushes pawns at your king, work out what the pawn push opens before you make an active move.

2. Before every move, check all your opponent's checks and captures, especially when you are under pressure.

3. Never stop looking for tactics: opponents blunder, and a stubborn defence gave you the win.

notes.14:
Q: Explain 7 qd6
After 7…Qd6, your queen was on a square where White could attack it with a developing move.

Look at the position first. White's knight on e5 was attacking your c6 knight, and your c6 knight was pinned. If it moves or is taken, the bishop on b5 gives check along the diagonal. Your move did two things. It guarded c6 again, but it put the queen on d6, where Bf4 hits it right away.

After 8.Bf4, your queen has to leave. White's Nxc6 then wins material, and the engine puts you about two pawns down.

The thinking error was checking only whether the knight was defended. You didn't ask what White's next move would attack. Before you play a queen move, look at which White pieces could hit that square with tempo.

The engine's better move was 7…Ne7. It adds a defender to c6 and unpins the knight. It also develops a piece and gets you ready to castle. After 8.O-O O-O 9.Nxc6 bxc6, your position is fine. The pawn structure is a bit bent, but you haven't lost material.

When a piece is under pressure, first look for a developing move that solves the problem. That is usually better than bringing the queen out early.

Q: Give me your best summary of your analysis of my play during this game
I only have data on one move, 7...Qd6, so this is a review of that moment and not the whole game.

Your opening was fine. Up to move 7 the position was roughly equal (-0.23). Then Qd6 turned it into a clear advantage for White (+2.16).

The thinking error was not asking what White's last move threatened. Ne5 and Bb5 were both aimed at your knight on c6, and the engine says White was threatening Nxc6. You moved the queen to a square that looked active, but it let White hit it with Bf4. After Bf4 Bxc3+ bxc3 Qa3 Nxc6 a6 Na7+, White comes out ahead in material, about 3 points within a few moves.

The better idea was Ne7. It adds a defender to the c6 knight and gets a piece developed. The line was Ne7 O-O O-O Nxc6 bxc6 Bd3 c5 a3, which is a normal, balanced position.

The habit to build is a quick checklist before every move. First, what is my opponent threatening? Second, which of my pieces are attacked or loosely defended? Third, can my new square be hit with a gain of tempo? Early queen moves often fail that third question.
notes.16:
Q: Explain8
Your idea with 8...f6 was natural: attack the knight on e5 and make it move. The mistake was not checking what the pawn move gives up.

Before moving, ask "what does this pawn stop protecting, and what lines does it open?" Moving the f-pawn opens the diagonal from h5 to your king on e8. White answered Qh5+. You have to stop the check, and after g6 White plays Nxg6. If hxg6, White's queen takes the rook on h8 with Qxh8. That's a rook lost, and your king is stuck in the middle.

When your king hasn't castled, every pawn move near it is a risk. Before any move, check all of White's checks and captures, even ones that look like they lose a piece.

The better move was 8...Ne7. It develops a piece, gets you closer to castling, and doesn't weaken your king. The engine line goes a3 Ba5 b4 Bc7 Bf4 Qd8 Nxc6. It's a little uncomfortable for you, but the position is roughly even.

Develop first, castle, and only then start pushing pawns.
notes.20:
Q: Why wasn't the best I've queen takes f4
Taking the bishop does win a piece, but it runs into a tactic. After 10... Qxf4, White plays Bxc6+. That's check, because the c6 pawn was the only thing shielding your king from the bishop on the diagonal. The bishop on c6 also attacks your rook on a8.

The engine's line continues 11... Kf7 12. Nxd5, with more threats against you. In the end White picks up your rook on a8 (Bxa8), and Stockfish rates the position +1.04 for White. That's slightly worse for you than the +0.87 after Qd7, so Qxf4 isn't better.

The thinking error here is easy to make. A free piece looks great, so you stop looking at what your own move uncovers. Before grabbing, ask what checks and captures the opponent gets afterwards. Here the c6 pawn and the bishop on b5 were the clue.

Qd7 keeps the queen safe and keeps the c6 pawn protected. It also stops Bxc6+ from working, because the queen guards c6.
notes.22:
Q: Explain 11
Engine verdict: 11…g6 is fine. It's just a little less accurate than the best move.

Your idea was sensible. You saw that White's queen could come to h5 with check, and you stopped that by playing g6. Looking for checks before you move is a good habit.

The problem is that g6 doesn't help your development. Your king is still in the middle, and your knight is still on g8 doing nothing. The pawn moves e6, f6 and g6 also leave dark squares weaker around your king. White's Qf3 is the engine's reply, and after it you're pushed into awkward king moves like Kf7 and Kg7. The evaluation moved from +0.88 to +1.33 for White.

The engine prefers 11…Ne7. That develops your worst piece first. If White plays Qh5+, you can answer g6 then, and the knight is already out. The engine's line goes Qh5+ g6 Qe2 Bd6 Qe3 Kf7, and your pieces are working together there.

The lesson is to ask what your least active piece is before you play a defensive pawn move. Often you can develop that piece and still deal with the threat.
notes.57:
Q: Explain why it's so bad
Qc6 is bad because White only looked at attacking and forgot to defend their own king.

Look at Black's pieces. The queen on h4 and the rook on f5 are both aimed at White's king side. The rook can swing to h5, and then Rh5 threatens mate on h2. Black's other rook can also join with Rd8, hitting the White queen.

White's queen was on d7 and did a useful job there. Qc6 moves it away from the king side, and it also drops the pressure on Black's king. After Rh5, White has to waste time on f3. Black then plays Rd8 and Qh2+, and the checks keep coming. The engine says Black is winning by about three pawns.

The thinking error is greed. Qc6 attacks the c5 pawn, but White didn't ask what Black was threatening. The engine says Black's threat was Rd8, and White's king was already exposed.

The better move was g3. It kicks the queen off the h-file and gives the king some air. The engine line goes g3 Qd4 Rad1, and White stays on top.

Before you grab a pawn, ask what your opponent's most dangerous move is, and whether your king is safe.
notes.60:
Q: Explain
Your move 30...Qd4+ is a classic case of "check because it's a check." You were clearly winning (the engine had you at about 77% winning chances). After Qd4+, White plays Rf2. That blocks the check and helps White's king. Your queen then has to run back with Qh4, and White plays Re2. The engine says that line ends in a repeating series of checks, so the position is level. You gave away a win.

The thinking error was not asking what White wanted to do. White was threatening Qe4, which would bring the queen back to the center and defend the king. A check doesn't stop that plan. It just forces White to make a move White was happy to make anyway.

The better idea was 30...Rd8. Your rook on a8 hadn't joined the attack yet. Rd8 brings it to the open d-file, where it can go to d2 or hit g2. The engine's line goes 31.Qe4 Qh2+ 32.Kf2 Rd2+ 33.Ke1 Rxg2 34.Qe3+. You keep attacking with all your pieces.

Before checking, ask yourself: what does my opponent want to do next, and does this move stop it? Also ask whether any of my pieces are still sitting out of the fight.

notes.27:
You were already better here, and 14.Na4 let most of it slip. Black's e6 pawn was doing two jobs: guarding d5 and guarding the knight on f5. 14.Nxd5! (which also hits the queen on b6) exd5 15.Qxf5 wins a clean pawn, because once the e-pawn takes on d5 it no longer protects f5.

Habit: captures first. Before a quiet move, look at every capture and ask who defends what. A pawn or piece guarding two things is the most common tactic at every level.
notes.31:
Your knight on c5 was attacked by the b6 pawn, and you counterattacked Black's knight with 16.b5. A counterattack only works if your threat is bigger. Here Black simply takes first (16...bxc5 17.bxc6), then ...Nxe3 and ...c4 hit your pieces with tempo, and ...Qxc6 wins your c6 pawn. Black ends up a pawn ahead with a protected passed pawn. Play the punishing line to see it.

Better: just move the knight. 16.Na6, hitting the queen, keeps the game balanced.

Habit: when a piece is attacked, deal with it first. Only counterattack after checking what happens if they just take.
notes.47:
This is the biggest moment of the game. 23...Bxa3 grabbed a pawn and attacked your rook on c1, and you moved the rook to c3. Look down the a-file instead: 24.Ra1! attacks the bishop, and Black's queen on a4 sits right behind it, so the bishop is pinned. It's attacked twice (rook and your queen on d3) and defended once. 24.Ra1 saves your rook and wins a whole piece.

After 24.Rc3, Black's bishop escapes with ...Bb4, hitting your rook again, and Black stays pawns up.

Habit: when you must move an attacked piece, check every square it can go to, especially squares that attack something.
notes.51:
Trading bishop for knight to double Black's h-pawns looks tempting, but your bishop on d2 had an important job: it controlled a5 and b4, the squares Black's passed a-pawn needed. After 26.Bxh6 nothing stops that pawn. The doubled h-pawns hardly matter; the a-pawn does.

Better: 26.Qb1, heading for b7 and the 7th rank.

Habit: before trading, ask what job your piece is doing.
notes.55:
Black had just misplaced the queen with 27...Qe8, and this was the moment to kill the passed a-pawn. Your rook was already on c7 eyeing a7; 28.Qa6 adds a second attacker and the pawn falls (for example 28...Bg5 29.Rxa7 Rxa7 30.Qxa7). After 28.Nd4, Black plays ...a5 and the pawn starts running.

Habit: passed pawns must be stopped or eaten. When your opponent has one, make it priority number one, especially when you're already attacking it.
notes.67:
Black had just walked the king to h5, out in the open, and the game was level. 34.Qe2+ checks that exposed king and keeps your own king safe. Instead 34.Kf3 put your king on the open files, and Black's queen swings to g8 and then comes into your position with checks. Black resigned or lost on time here, but on the board Black was winning.

Habit: in queen-and-rook positions, look for checks against an exposed king first, and keep your own king tucked away.

meta.summary:
You came out of the Caro-Kann Advance with a good position and were clearly better by move 14. From there the game swung back and forth: both sides made several serious errors, and Black was ahead for most of the last 20 moves before the game ended in your favor.

Two moments decided most of it. On move 16 you counterattacked instead of saving your attacked knight, and on move 24 you missed 24.Ra1, a pin that would have won a whole bishop. After that, Black's passed a-pawn became the main story, and you traded away the bishop that held it.

1. Check what your opponent's last move threatens before every move.
2. Look at all captures and attacks, for both sides, before choosing a quiet move.
3. Stop or win passed pawns before anything else.
